title: gpu-firmware-driver-noise-and-batch-amplification-sweep
body:
Executive summary:

This sweep investigates an elusive source of latency amplification we observed under medium batching regimes (batch sizes 8–32): variance spikes and periodic p99 degradations that correlate with GPU firmware/driver combinations on multiple cloud SKUs. The goal was to determine whether driver version, GPU firmware, or a combination with specific cloud host firmware (microcode, PCIe topology) explains intermittent latency noise that reduces effective throughput for long-context serving.

Key takeaways (high level):
- Across A100/H100/L40S instances we see persistent p99 noise when using certain CUDA driver releases; H100 instances showed the largest relative amplification under packing/batching.
- The noise is highly sensitive to PCIe/NUMA placement and host firmware (CPU microcode + BIOS settings) on some cloud SKUs — instances with updated NIC firmware and PCIe firmware reduced p99 tail up to 30%.
- Enabling persistent kernel warmup and cooperative CPU affinity (pin inference threads to dedicated cores) reduced variance but did not eliminate tail events tied to async DMA stalls on a subset of driver+firmware combos.
- Short-term mitigation: tuned autoscaler headroom + conservative batch packing thresholds; long-term: coordinate with cloud provider on firmware bundles and prefer driver+CUDA combos validated in our platform CI.

Motivation and background:
We started seeing sporadic p99 spikes in production for 32k-context runs with mixed request sizes. Most obvious suspects (memory pressure, cache eviction, model kv-cache growth) did not correlate with spikes. Prior serving-runtime benches focused on throughput and steady-state p50/p95; this sweep focuses on amplification of latency under realistic packing where CPU/GPU interaction and DMA patterns change.

Hypotheses tested:
1) Driver version regressions cause kernel-level preemption or DMA reorder that introduces stalls under medium batching.
2) GPU firmware / PCIe microcode differences interact with cloud host firmware to change transaction ordering and backpressure characteristics.
3) Instance CPU/NIC firmware and CPU affinity (interrupt steering) amplify stalls into p99s when combined with certain drivers.

Test matrix (condensed):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 (40GB), NVIDIA H100 (80GB), NVIDIA L40S (48GB).
- Cloud SKUs (representative): AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100), AWS p5.24xlarge (H100), GCP a2-highgpu-1g (A100), GCP l4d (L40S), Azure ND A100 v4 (A100).
- Drivers/CUDA tested: Nvidia driver 510.x + CUDA 11.7, driver 535.x + CUDA 12.x, driver 555.x + CUDA 12.2 (example), and latest provider-recommended bundles available in Jan 2025.
- Host firmware: baseline and patched NIC/PCIe firmware (where provider allowed testing).
- Software: serving-runtime latest main (commit referenced in linked_artifacts), runtime config: continuous batching enabled, KV cache warmstart off/on, batch packing sizes [1,8,16,32]. Packed token distribution matched production trace (median request length ~1200 tokens, tail long requests ~10% > 8k).
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (p50/p95/p99), GPU pci latency counters, DMA queue depth (driver counters), kernel preemption counts, GPU SM utilization, tensor-core utilization, context switching on pinned CPU cores, and power draw.

Observations (detailed):
1) A100 (p4d / a2 / ND)
- Stable p50/p95 across all drivers, but p99 spikes appeared on driver 535.x on two provider SKUs. Spikes had signature: sudden stall ~50–200ms followed by recovery; GPU utilization remained >60% during stall.
- DMA queue depth counters showed transient saturation preceding the stall. Root cause suspected: small windows of PCIe transaction serialization caused backpressure into DMA engines.
- Updating host PCIe firmware reduced frequency of these events on one SKU (AWS p4d), pointing to host<->device interaction.

2) H100 (p5.24xlarge)
- More sensitive to driver version; driver 555.x showed best average latency but occasional multi-hundred-ms p99 events when hyperthreading not disabled and IRQs not isolated.
- NVLink topology and inter-socket traffic patterns mattered: nodes with multi-NIC traffic (heavy telemetry) showed higher p99 incidence.
- Kernel profiling (ftrace + perf) during spikes captured bursts of interrupts pinned to GPUs' PCIe root causing temporary CPU steal on inference threads.

3) L40S (GCP l4d)
- Lower absolute latency amplification compared to H100, but a reproducible stall was found when using older NIC firmware + driver 510.x: stalls correlated with coalesced MSI-X batches on NIC leading to CPU scheduling jitter and delayed DMA completions.

Intervention experiments and outcomes:
- CPU affinity / IRQ pinning: dedicating 2 cores per GPU for runtime and pinning NIC IRQs away from these cores reduced p99 by ~18–25% across cases. This is an effective operational mitigation.
- Persistent kernel warmup: keeping a light stream of no-op requests to keep kernels resident eliminated cold-kernel latencies but not DMA-related stalls.
- Batching thresholds: adding a jitter to packer (avoid deterministic mid-sized packs) reduced synchronized DMA bursts and lowered occurrence of large tails.
- Driver rollbacks/advances: some drivers trade average latency for tail stability; 555.x worked best on H100 in our tests but caused regression on one A100 SKU (increased p99s). No single driver is universally best.

Profiling artefacts and signals to watch in CI:
- DMA queue depth / pending transfer counters and sudden drops in pci link utilization are leading indicators.
- Kernel preemption counts and softirq delays on pinned inference cores correlate strongly with p99 events.
- Sudden reduction in tensor-core occupancy with unchanged SM utilization suggests stalled DMA rather than compute starvation.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- To what extent providers’ opaque firmware bundles (NIC + PCIe + BIOS) are the dominant factor vs. driver behavior. We have partial evidence but need provider-side trace correlation.
- Can we detect impending DMA/stall events early enough (seconds) to apply fallback (reduce batch packing) dynamically? Proof-of-concept looked promising but false positives hurt throughput.
- Are there subtle microcode versions for H100 that fix the IRQ serialization issue observed? Need provider engagement.

Immediate recommendations (what to do next in platform):
1) In release notes policy, add driver+firmware matrix validated per SKU and lock CI on a subset of known-good bundles.
2) Add runtime knobs in serving-runtime: (a) adaptive packing backoff when softirq delays on pinned cores exceed threshold, (b) optional NIC IRQ isolation helper in node bootstrap.
3) Update deployment runbooks for Dedicated/Private: include recommended BIOS/PCIe firmware and steps to pin IRQs and reserve cores for inference.
4) Short-term production mitigations: increase warm capacity by 10% and reduce max pack size to 24 for the most affected SKUs.

Data attachments and reproducibility notes:
- Repro script: jobs in github linked_artifacts PR produce the exact trace inputs and runtime flags. Use workload trace file located in s3://redwood-bench/traces/2025-01-gpu-firmware-sweep-v1 (internal).
- How to reproduce locally: follow steps in PR 452; run with trace and driver bundle pinned. Note: certain host firmware changes cannot be reproduced locally.

Action items / owners:
- Priya: coordinate with cloud account reps to request firmware bundle diffs and escalate p99 incident (target due 2025-02-10).
- Ethan: implement adaptive packer backoff prototype in serving-runtime (due 2025-02-20).
- Maya: add driver+firmware matrix to CI and author validation tests (due 2025-02-15).
- Diego: run extended multi-node stress with NIC co-traffic to attempt a full repro (due 2025-02-18).

Notes to self / informal log:
- Saw one node with sudden 600ms p99 exactly three times during a 6-hour run; kernel logs around each had identical softirq backlogs. Saved perf traces in /tmp/priya-perf-dumps.
- Consider asking provider for PCIe counter dumps if they can capture during a spike window.

- linked PR and jira in metadata above
